articles.title: Reproducible builds for obfuscated .NET assemblies
articles.excerpt: Deterministic compilation is one of the quieter wins of modern .NET. Turn on true — it is the default for SDK-style projects — and Roslyn will emit a byte-identical assembly from identical source, ide…
articles.body: Deterministic compilation is one of the quieter wins of modern .NET. Turn on <Deterministic>true</Deterministic> — it is the default for SDK-style projects — and Roslyn will emit a byte-identical assembly from identical source, identical references and an identical compiler. No wall-clock timestamp, no random module GUID. Two engineers on two machines get the same DLL, and CI can prove the shipped binary matches the source. Then you run it through an obfuscator, and the guarantee evaporates. Hash the protected assembly from two consecutive runs of the exact same inputs and you get two different hashes. Nothing about your code changed. So where did the determinism go? The real question An obfuscator reads an assembly, rewrites its metadata and IL, and writes a new assembly.

articles.excerpt: Publicado originalmente en juliancardozo.github.io. Un modelo de lenguaje, por sí solo, es una función estocástica: recibe contexto y devuelve una muestra. Un agente es esa función dentro de un loop c…
articles.body: Publicado originalmente en juliancardozo.github.io . Un modelo de lenguaje, por sí solo, es una función estocástica: recibe contexto y devuelve una muestra. Un agente es esa función dentro de un loop con herramientas, memoria y un criterio de parada. Y un sistema multiagente es otra cosa: una arquitectura distribuida donde varias de esas inferencias se reparten el trabajo, comparten estado y se controlan entre sí. Website Factory es un ejemplo completo y público: un orquestador de Claude Code descompone un objetivo, lo delega en seis subagentes especializados sobre el flujo Spec-Driven Development de GitHub Spec Kit y solo da una etapa por cerrada cuando un verificador determinista lo confirma. Entrada: un brief en Markdown.

articles.body: Before you picture a sci-fi receptionist, picture your inbox at eleven at night: three people asking about your opening hours, one asking whether an item ships abroad, one complaining that an order arrived late. None of those needed you. That is the gap an AI chatbot fills for a business with a handful of employees — not a replacement for judgment, but a filter that keeps judgment for the messages that deserve it. What a bot actually replaces — and what it must never touch A full-time support agent costs somewhere between $3,500 and $5,500 per month, and for most operations under fifty employees that line item was never realistic.

articles.body: Your page ranks on Google. ChatGPT still ignores it. Here's the checklist I use A page can sit near the top of Google and still get zero citations from ChatGPT, Perplexity, or Doubao. I ran into this gap while working through a real question: why does good SEO not turn into AI visibility? The short answer is that ranking and being cited are different jobs. Ranking is about being found and ordered. Being cited is about being usable as evidence in an answer. That split is worth checking in order, not all at once. If you skip ahead to "write more content," you can spend weeks fixing the wrong stage. 1. Can the AI crawler even get in? Start here because it is the easiest stage to prove, and the easiest to get wrong. Check robots.txt first, but read it carefully.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 16, 1974: The giant Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico broadcasts humanity's 1st interstellar message
articles.excerpt: On this day in space! Nov. 16, 1974: The giant Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico broadcasts humanity's 1st interstellar message
articles.body: On Nov. 16, 1974, humans sent their first message to the stars in an attempt to contact extraterrestrials. They did this using what was then the largest radio telescope in the world, located at the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico. A group of scientists led by Frank Drake and Carl Sagan sent their message to the M13 star cluster . The message was written in binary code and contained information about human DNA. It also included figures of a human, the solar system and the Arecibo telescope. The idea was that if any aliens were to receive the signal and figure out how to decode it, they would know where it came from. Because M13 is 25,000 light-years away, it will take 25,000 years for any M13 aliens to hear our message — if they are even out there.

articles.title: Relive Starship’s historic Flight 15 with our best photos from launch and ‘Mechazilla’ tower catch
articles.excerpt: See the most epic photos from SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 test flight and historic launch tower catch.
articles.body: STARBASE, Texas — SpaceX has officially wrapped up the 15th test flight of its massive Starship rocket, successfully catching the vehicle's upper stage for the first time. Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX's Starbase facility here in South Texas on Friday (Nov. 13). The mission was billed as the first to bring both of Starship's stages, the Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage, back to the launch site for recovery. And, while SpaceX was forced to divert Super Heavy's return to an off-shore splashdown (and explosion), the upper stage managed to survive its 22-hour jaunt in orbit and plunge through the atmosphere for a picture-perfect catch by the launch tower back at Starbase.

articles.title: Elon Musk says SpaceX’s Starship, already the largest rocket on Earth, will get even bigger with next-gen V4 model
articles.excerpt: Just a day after SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship megarocket back at the launch pad for the first time ever, Elon Musk told us that the spacecraft will get even bigger.
articles.body: As usual, SpaceX and its founder Elon Musk are thinking big. The company recovered the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever on Saturday (Nov. 14), plucking it out of the sky with the "chopstick" arms of its Texas launch tower. It was a huge moment for SpaceX , bringing its vision of full and rapid rocket reuse much closer to reality. But Elon Musk isn't one to dwell on the past or rest on laurels, so he soon outlined an even more ambitious future for Starship. "Starship V4 will be ~70m [230 feet] long, which is roughly a 40% length increase and allows >60% more propellant load," Musk said via X, the social media platform he owns, on Sunday evening (Nov. 15).
